newsitem.title: CONGO: UN gets first public offers for Congo peace force.
newsitem.headline: UN gets first public offers for Congo peace force.

text.p: Senegal and Togo offered troops for a Congo Republic peacekeeping force which a U.N. envoy said could be in place swiftly to try to prevent a ceasefire from breaking down.

A 90-minute artillery duel on Monday between pro- and anti-president factions almost derailed a six-day-old truce but, after what the French ambassador called "a stormy day" in the capital Brazzaville, fighting subsided again.

The fighting, which wounded at least seven people and risked embroiling the nearby Democratic Republic of Congo (formerly Zaire) when seven shells crashed near its capital Kinshasa across the Congo River from Brazzaville, underlined the urgency of getting the intervention force in place.

Mohamed Sahnoun, the U.N. envoy for Congo and the former Zaire, said after a summit of eight west African states in Togo that a force of an initial 1,600-1,800 men could be deployed rapidly in Brazzaville. But he said it would not stay indefinitely.
Mediators want the intervention force to help restore conditions so that democratic presidential elections, which were to have been held on July 27, can go ahead.
Brazzaville descended into warfare on June 5 when President Pascal Lissouba tried to disarm a militia run by his predecessor and now rival candidate for the elections, Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Until the flare-up, the sleepy city of a million had seemed like a haven of peace to people across the river in teeming Kinshasa, who had feared their own war as Laurent Kabila's rebels neared to finish off the rule of Zairean dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, who has since fled into exile.
Kabila's foreign minister said he believed the country has been deliberately targeted in Monday's shelling, which state television said wounded one man inside the former Zaire.

"We could tell precisely where they were fired from," Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha said, without identified the guilty party. He gave a "final warning" that the country would defend itself if there were any further such incidents.
The truce dampened fighting that raged for 12 days in the former French colonial capital Brazzaville, killing an estimated 1,000 people. Sahnoun said even more could have died.
But no day has gone by without some firing, blamed by mediators on rogue elements in the two rival forces.
Monday's battle was the worst breach of the truce.
At least two shells slammed into houses near a crowded market in Bacongo suburb, until now a comparatively calm refuge inside the city and controlled by a neutral militia.
Panicky civilians, fearing the war was spreading, piled into trucks and left for the rural hinterland, which has been untouched by the fighting.
